rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The subject of يربو is the riba mentioned earlier; an omitted noun is understood, meaning acquisition or attraction of people’s wealth.
rows.anchor: هذا كله كلام أبي علي ذكره في مواضع متفرقة

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ reads لتربوا with a damma on the tāʾ: you become owners of an increase from people’s wealth by attracting it through what you give.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع: (لتربوا) بالتاء وضمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gift does not grow with God because its giver sought increased return, not God’s good pleasure and nearness; a gift seeking God’s face would be different.
rows.anchor: لأنكم إنما قصدتم إلى زيادة العوض، ولم تقصدوا وجه البر والقربة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The second ما can be relative and nominative; آتيتم is its relative clause, with an omitted object pronoun understood as آتيتموه.
rows.anchor: هذا كله كلام أبي علي ذكره في مواضع متفرقة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The wording shifts from direct address to third person, as in 10:22, moving from وما آتيتم to فأولئك.
rows.anchor: هذا كله كلام أبي علي ذكره في مواضع متفرقة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The فاء follows because the relative clause contains a verb; the predicate is understood as you are those with multiplied reward, with a deleted resumptive pronoun, as in the idiom السمن منوان بدرهم.
rows.anchor: هذا كله كلام أبي علي ذكره في مواضع متفرقة

words: وَمَآ ءَاتَيْتُم مِّن زَكَوٰةٍۢ تُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Charity is given without seeking repayment and with the aim of what is with God; its people receive multiplied reward, tenfold for each good deed.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: وما أعطيتم من صدقة لا تطلبون بها المكافأة وإنما تقصدون بها ما عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: المضعفون can mean possessors of many good deeds, like مقو meaning strong or موسر meaning wealthy: people with multiplied rewards.
rows.anchor: وكذلك: مضعف، ذو أضعاف من الحسنات

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil introduces the following passage as describing what befell people because they abandoned monotheism.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: ثم ذكر ما أصاب الناس من ترك التوحيد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says this is an admonition urging them to be wary.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: ثم وعظهم ليحذروا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the water brought to the land as a torrent.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد السيل

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj define al-jurz as land that does not grow vegetation; the word has four dialectal vocalizations, like al-shughl and al-bukhl.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج: هي التي لا تنبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary has already discussed the meaning and derivation of al-jurz under the Cave sūra’s verse 8.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا تفسير الجرز واشتقاقه في سورة الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies a particular land in Yemen without seas or rivers; unexpected torrents reach it, allowing people to sow whatever grain they wish.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد أرضا باليمن ليس فيها بحار ولا أنهار

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid describes land that grows only when it receives floodwater rather than rain.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هي أرض (¬7)

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda locates al-jurz in the region of Aden, treating it as a particular place.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول أبي عبيدة قال: إنها بناحية عدن

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says that if al-jurz is a place-name for a particular land, the definite article is linguistically unexpected for a proper name; it is possible for names originally used as shared descriptions, like al-Madīna and al-Baṣra.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد (¬2): على هذا القول إنها أرض بعينها

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains the article in transferred descriptive names as retaining a notional trace of the description when it becomes a proper name.
rows.anchor: وسبب دخول اللام على هذه الأسماء مع كونها معارف أنها أوصاف نقلت فصارت أعلاما

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says it is dead land without vegetation until water arrives and produces plants eaten by people and animals; Muqātil gives a similar explanation.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي في هذه الآية: هي الأرض الميتة التي لا نبات لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suddī’s general reading is better because it matches the nearby argument against deniers of resurrection: God revives dead land; the passage names no particular place.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول كان أجود؛ لأنه أشبه بنظائر هذه الآية من الاحتجاج على منكري البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the general reading of dead land, the water may be rain or a torrent.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا القول قوله: {الماء إلى الأرض الجرز} يجوز أن يكون المطر ويجوز أن يكون يريد السيل

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī takes abundant remembrance to mean remembrance with the tongue.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي ومقاتل: ذكرا كثيرا باللسان

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil also takes abundant remembrance to mean remembrance with the tongue.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي ومقاتل: ذكرا كثيرا باللسان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains it as never forgetting God.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو ألا ينساه أبدا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī also explains abundant remembrance as the five daily prayers.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: ويعني ذكرا كثيرا بالصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: ابن حيان
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥayyān says it is glorifying, praising, declaring God’s oneness and greatness in every situation, with the formulas subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu li-llāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن حيان: هو التسبيح والتحميد والتهليل والتكبير على كل حال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report received by the author says that a person in major ritual impurity, after relieving himself, or in a state of minor impurity may say these remembrance formulas.
rows.anchor: وبلغنا أن هؤلاء الكلمات يتكلم بهن صاحب الجنابة والغائط والحدث

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil explains morning and evening glorification as the dawn and afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: صلاة الفجر والعصر. قاله مقاتل وقتادة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda likewise explains the command as the dawn and afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: صلاة الفجر والعصر. قاله مقاتل وقتادة

rows.speaker: ابن حيان
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥayyān glosses the command as praying to God in the morning and evening.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن حيان: صلوا لله بالغداة # والعشي

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī identifies bukra with dawn prayer and aṣīl with the noon, afternoon, sunset, and night prayers.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: فصلاة الفجر، وأما أصيلا: فصلاة الظهر والعصر والمغرب والعشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary’s discussion of aṣīl was given under the phrase بالغدو والآصال.
rows.anchor: ومضى الكلام في تفسير الأصيل عند قوله: {بالغدو والآصال}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave David a favor from Himself.
rows.anchor: أي: أعطيناه من عندنا فضلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God bestowed on David what He had given to no one before or after him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد تفضلت عليه وأعطيته ما لم أعط أحدا قبله ولا بعده

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil identifies the favor as prophethood and scripture.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يعني بالفضل: النبوة والكتاب

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī identifies the favor as prophethood and the worldly gifts David received.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: يعني: النبوة وما أعطي من الدنيا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والزجاج
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Zajjāj treat the wording as elliptical: God said, “Mountains, echo back praise with him.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة والزجاج: هو مختصر، المعنى: وقلنا يا جبال {أوبي معه}

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes unanimously explain awibi maʿahu as glorify along with David.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون كلهم: سبحي معه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq derives awibi from āba yaʾūbu, to return: the mountains return the glorification with David.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: أوبي معه معناه: رجعى، يقال: آب يؤوب إذا رجع

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: An unnamed alternative takes taʾwīb in Arabic as traveling all day until night, so the mountains praise with David throughout the day.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: التأويب في كلام العرب. سير النهار كله إلى الليل

rows.speaker: سلامة بن جندل
rows.claim: Salāma b. Jandal’s verse uses taʾwīb for a day of travel toward the enemy, witnessing this travel sense.
rows.anchor: قال سلامة بن جندل: يومان يوم مقامات وأندية ... ويوم سير إلى الأعداء تأويب

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr defines taʾwīb as traveling during the day and camping at night, in a report transmitted by Abū ʿUbayda.
rows.anchor: روى أبو عبيد عن أبي عمرو: التأويب أن يسير النهار وينزل الليل

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba prefers the all-day-travel interpretation: the mountains praise with David until night; al-Rāʿī’s verse supports the sense of continuing a journey.
rows.anchor: وهذا اختيار ابن قتيبة، (وأنشد للراعي فقال:

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes report that when David glorified, the mountains glorified along with him.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: وكانت إذا سبح داود سبحت الجبال معه

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb reports that when David called, the mountains answered with their echoes, which is the echo people hear.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب (¬3): كان داود إذا نادى أجابته الجبال بصداها

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: One of Abū Isḥāq’s parses coordinates al-ṭayr with faḍlan: God gave David favor and subjected the birds for him.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أن يكون عطفا على قوله فضلا (¬5)، كأنه آتينا داود فضلا والطير

rows.speaker: يونس عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Yūnus transmits this coordination parse from Abū ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وروى هذا يونس عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains the coordination as in the idiom, “I fed him food and gave him water.”
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء في هذا الوجه هو كقولك: أطعمته طعاما وسقيته ماء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says the accusative is like the vocative construction yā Zayd wa-al-Ṣalt aqbilā.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: زعم النحويون أن سبيل نصبها كقولك: يا زيد والصلت أقبلا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the second vocative is accusative because it lacks the vocative particle and is treated as diverted from its normal vocative form.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: نصبت الصلة؛ لأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third parse makes al-ṭayr accusative by the implied maʿa, meaning the mountains and birds echo praise with David; the author calls Abū Isḥāq’s three parses the most apt.
rows.anchor: الوجه الثالث: أن يكون الطير منصوبا على موضع مع، كما تقول: قمت وزيدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the birds glorified with David when he glorified.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كانت الطير تسبح معه إذا سبح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the iron became like wax in David’s hand.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: حتى صار عنده مثل السمع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says David could take iron in his hand and it became like dough.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: كان يأخذ الحديد بيده، فيصير كأنه عجين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God softened iron for David, who worked it without fire.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ألان (¬10) الله له الحديد

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash says the iron was softened until it was like threads.
rows.anchor: وقال الأعمش: ألين له حتى كان مثل الخيوط

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says David made linked coats of mail without tools or fire, completing one in part of a day or night worth one thousand dirhams.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: كان داود يسرد الدرع لا يفرغها بحديد ولا يدخلها النار

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq treats أن as explanatory: God softened iron so David could make ample coats of mail; an explanatory particle may introduce an imperative, as in “send to him that he rise.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أن اعمل هاهنا في تأويل التفسير، كأنه قيل: وألنا له الحديد

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says sabagha describes a coat or anything long enough to reach the ground; it is used of abundant rain and a plentiful blessing too.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: سبغت الدرع، وكل شيء طال إلى الأرض فهو سابغ

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: A Hudhalī poet’s phrase al-sawābigh witnesses the use of the word for ample coats of mail.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول الهذلي (¬5): أو صنع السوابغ تبع

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr’s verse describes a sabigha coat covering the fingers like a pool of clear water.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله بن الزبير: وسابغة تغشى البنان كأنها ... أضاة بضحضاح من الماء ظاهر.

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says sabighāt omits the described noun, coats of mail, because the adjective makes that noun understood; a sabigh garment covers what lies beneath and extends beyond it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (ومعنى سابغات: أي: دروع سابغات، فذكر الصفة؛ لأنها تدل على الموصوف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the sabighāt as iron coats of mail.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: في قوله: {أن اعمل سابغات} يريد: دروع الحديد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says these were long coats of mail; before David, armor was made of hammered iron plates.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يعني: الدروع الطوال، وكانت الدروع قبل داود إنما هي صفائح الحديد مضروبة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses it as in the making or links of the armor, and calls a coat dirʿ masrūda; Abū Dhuʾayb’s verse uses masrūdatān.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: (في سردها، يقال: درع مسرودة. وقال أبو ذؤيب: وعليهما مسرودتان

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says sard is a collective name for coats of mail and similar craftwork, called so because the ends of links are pierced and joined with nails.
rows.anchor: وقال الليث: (السرد: اسم جامع للدروع وما أشبهها من عمل الخلق

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba glosses sard as the joining or weaving of armor; the armor-maker is called a sarrād or zarrād, with sīn alternating with zāy.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن، قتيبة: [والسرد: سجع المدرع]

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says sard is the fastening of nails, and a masrūda coat is armor whose nails have been secured well; al-Aʿshā’s verse attests the term.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: السرد نقب المسامير، يقال: درع مسرودة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj defines sard as arranging things successively so each trace follows the last; the same root describes continuous speech and fasting, three consecutive sacred months, and a row of connected fastenings.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (السرد في اللغة: مقدمة شيء إلى شيء حتى ينسق أثره في أثر بعض سابغا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In Mujāhid’s transmission, Ibn ʿAbbās says not to make nails thin and rings wide so the armor loosens, or nails thick and rings narrow so they break; make them proportionate.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية مجاهد: لا تدق المسامير وتوسع الحلق فيسلس، ولا يغلظ المسامير

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba says sard means the nails in the mail links; the author says this best fits the interpretation shared by all exegetes, who discuss sizing the nails to avoid looseness or breakage.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: السرد: المسامير التي في حلق الدرع (¬4). وهذا هو الأشبه بالمعنى

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says to size the nails for the links: oversized nails split them, while undersized ones slip loose.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يقول قدر المسامير في الحلق، ولا تعظمه فينفصم، ولا تصغره فيسلس

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says not to pair a thick nail with a narrow hole or a thin nail with a wide hole; make the construction balanced and suited to its need.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (وهو أن لا يجعل المسمار غليظا والثقب دقيقا، ولا يجعل المسمار دقيقا

rows.speaker: مقاتل وابن عباس
rows.claim: Muqātil says God then commands David’s household to act righteously; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses this as thanking God as He deserves.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل (¬8): ثم قال الله لآل داود: {واعملوا صالحا إني بما تعملون بصير} قال ابن عباس: يريدوا اشكروا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary says its explanation of “If He wills, He can remove you” was given previously, and continues through the clause about a burdened soul.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {إن يشأ يذهبكم} مفسر فيما مضى (¬5) إلى قوله: {وإن تدع مثقلة}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads the phrase as a soul burdened with sins calling for help with its burden.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج: أي وإن تدع نفس مثقلة بالذنوب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj likewise explains it as a soul weighed down by sins calling for help.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء والزجاج: أي وإن تدع نفس مثقلة بالذنوب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says nafs is grammatically used for either a male or a female, as in “Every soul tastes death” (3:185).
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (والنفس تعبر عن الذكر والأنثى، كقوله (¬1): {كل نفس ذائقة الموت}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden is the sins and transgressions carried by the soul.
rows.anchor: أي: ما حمل من الخطايا والذنوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “none of it will be carried” refers to that soul’s burden.
rows.anchor: {لا يحمل منه} أي: من حملها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says even a close relation carries none of another person’s sins.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: ولو كان بينهما ما حملت عنها شيء من وزرها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās pictures the burdened person asking her son to carry some of her load, while he replies that he has enough of his own.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يقول: يا بني احمل عني، فيقول: حسبي ما علي

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the close relation can be a father, son, or someone similar.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: أي ولو كان الذي يدعوه ذا قربى، مثل الأب والابن

words: إِنَّمَا تُنذِرُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلْغَيْبِ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says these are God’s allies, who fear Him and fear His punishment though it is unseen to them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد أولياؤه

words: إِنَّمَا تُنذِرُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُم بِٱلْغَيْبِ
rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the warning benefits only those who fear their Lord; it is as though the Prophet warns them rather than those whom warning cannot benefit, as in 79:45.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: تأويله أن إنذارك إنما ينفع الذين يخشون ربهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains purification as finding guidance, which benefits the person himself.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: من اهتدى فإنما يهتدي لنفسه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil explains it as becoming righteous; that righteousness benefits the person himself.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: من صلح فصلاحه لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All return to God, who will recompense people for their deeds in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: فيجزي بالأعمال في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The living are believers and the dead are disbelievers.
rows.anchor: يعني: المؤمنين والكافرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a disbeliever is like a dead person despite eating, drinking, coming, and going; he cites “dead, not living” (16:21).
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: الكافر وإن كان يأكل ويشرب ويجيء ويذهب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God enables His allies—those created for Paradise and protected from disbelief—to hear.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يسمع أولياءه (¬1) الذين خلقهم لجنته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God lets whomever He wills hear His words so that they take heed and find guidance.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: يسمع كلامه من يشاء حتى يتعظ يهتدي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī explains “He makes hear” as “He guides whom He wills.”
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: يهدي من يشاء

words: وَمَآ أَنتَ بِمُسْمِعٍۢ مَّن فِى ٱلْقُبُورِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those in graves represent disbelievers: they are like the dead because they are deaf to and do not answer the call to faith.
rows.anchor: يعني: الكفار، شبههم حين صموا ولم يجيبوا إذا دعوا إلى الإيمان بأهل القبور

words: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَٱلدَّوَآبِّ وَٱلْأَنْعَٰمِ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَٰنُهُۥ
rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj supplies an ellipsis: among what God created are people, animals, and livestock of differing colors, as with the fruits and mountains.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: المعنى: وفيما خلقنا مختلفا ألوانه من الناس والدواب والأنعام

words: إِنَّمَا يَخْشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ ٱلْعُلَمَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil say the clause uses fronting and postponement, placing the object before the subject.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي ومقاتل: في هذه الآية تقديم وتأخير (¬2). يعنيان تقديم المفعول على الفاعل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says those who fear God are the people who know His omnipotence, might, and sovereignty.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد إنما يخافني من خلقي من علم جبروتي وعزتي وسلطاني

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says those who know God best fear Him most.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: أشد الناس لله خشية أعلمهم به

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the scholars of God are the people who fear Him.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: العلماء بالله هم الذين يخشونه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says fear of God suffices as knowledge, while feeling secure from God is ignorance.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: كفى بخشية الله علما

rows.speaker: مجاهد والشعبي
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Shaʿbī define a scholar as one who fears God.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والشعبي: العالم من خاف الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil say God is mighty in His dominion and forgiving toward believers’ sins.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومقاتل: عزيز في ملكه، غفور لذنوب المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the people of monotheism, the community of Muḥammad, ends here; the passage now describes the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: فلما بلغ هذا الموضع انقطعت صفة أهل التوحيد، وهم أمة محمد -صلى الله عليه وسلم-، ثم قال في صفة الكفار

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses femūtū as the response to the negation: death is not decreed for them so that they might die.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: فيموتوا جواب النفي، المعنى: لا يقضى عليهم الموت فيموتوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, lā yuqḍā ʿalayhim can mean they are not destroyed, as in Moses striking a man and killing him (28:15); this reading needs no omitted word.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون معنى لا يقضى عليهم لا يهلكون، من قوله: {فوكزه موسى فقضى عليه}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says they would die and find relief from the torment they endure.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: فيموتوا فيستريحوا مما (¬9) هم فيه من العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment is not lightened for even the blink of an eye.
rows.anchor: {ولا يخفف عنهم من عذابها} طرفة عين كذلك يعن ما ذكر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil gloss every kafūr as every disbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس ومقاتل: هكذا نجزي كل كفور كل كافر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains reviving the dead as resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد البعث

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says what people sent ahead includes good and evil deeds and what later people followed from them; al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj choose this view.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: من خير أو شر فاقتدى بها (¬2) من بعدهم. وهذا اختيار الفراء والزجاج

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr says their traces are practices they instituted.
rows.anchor: وهو قول سعيد بن جبير، قال: {وآثارهم}: ما سنوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ’s transmission, Ibn ʿAbbās explains traces as the good or evil legacy someone leaves, as in 75:13.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: ما آثروا من أثر خير أو شر

rows.speaker: أنس وابن عباس في رواية عكرمة
rows.claim: Anas and Ibn ʿAbbās, in ʿIkrima’s transmission, report that the verse was revealed about Banū Salima, who considered moving closer to the Prophet’s mosque but stayed after its revelation; traces here are their footsteps.
rows.anchor: وقال أنس وابن عباس في رواية عكرمة: نزلت هذه الآية في بني سلمة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan also explains their traces as their footsteps.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن (¬1)، ومجاهد في رواية ابن أبي نجيح (¬2)، وقتادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد عن ابن أبي نجيح
rows.claim: Mujāhid, in Ibn Abī Najīḥ’s transmission, also explains their traces as their footsteps.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن (¬1)، ومجاهد في رواية ابن أبي نجيح (¬2)، وقتادة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda also explains their traces as their footsteps.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الحسن (¬1)، ومجاهد في رواية ابن أبي نجيح (¬2)، وقتادة

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz says that if God were to leave any human trace unrecorded, it would be the trace winds rub away.
rows.anchor: وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز: لو كان الله تاركا لابن آدم شيئا لترك ما عبث (¬4) عليه الرياح من أثر

rows.speaker: مسروق
rows.claim: Masrūq says every step a person takes is recorded as either a good deed or a sin.
rows.anchor: وقال مسروق: ما خطأ رجل خطوة إلا كتب حسنة أو سيئة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says what they sent ahead is good, while their traces are the misguidance and practice of error they leave behind.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد قال: ما قدموا من خير، وآثارهم: وما أورثوا من الضلالة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says readers agree on the accusative kull because the verb’s object pronoun refers back to it; a nominative is also possible as a new sentence.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: القراء يجمعون على نصب كل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ compares the accusative construction to “I struck Zayd and spoke to ʿAmr,” where the later noun remains accusative after the preceding verb; here too a verb precedes it.
rows.anchor: والاختيار أن يقول: (¬2) ضربت زيدا وعمرا كلمته، ينتصب عمرا لسبق الفعل قبله

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows nominative kull if the phrase is treated as a fresh sentence.
rows.anchor: وهو قوله: {ونكتب ما قدموا}. ويجوز الرفع على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says God made clear every deed that He recorded.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: {وكل شيء} من الأعمال ما (¬4) {أحصيناه} بيناه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses aḥṣaynāhu as “We preserved it.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: حفظناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥṣāʾ means counting, and counting can mean either making something clear or preserving it.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الإحصاء في اللغة: العد، والعد يكون للبيان ويكون للحفظ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil identify the clear register as the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومقاتل: في اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies it as the Mother of the Book.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: يعني أم الكتاب

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The scholars of meaning say this register lets the angels compare it with events as they occur and demonstrates God’s detailed knowledge.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني (¬9): وفي ذلك اعتبار الملائكة إذ قابلوا به ما يحدث # من الأمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qamar is read in both the nominative and accusative, with several syntactic analyses for each case.
rows.anchor: قرئ: والقمر بالرفع والنصب

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق وأبو علي
rows.claim: The nominative can estimate “and a sign for them is the moon,” as with the night and sun passages, or treat the moon as subject and qaddarnāhu as its predicate.
rows.anchor: فالرفع بتقدير: وآية لهم القمر، كما ذكرنا في قوله: {الليل نسلخ} و {والشمس تجري}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق وأبو علي
rows.claim: The accusative can treat the phrase as “We measured the moon; We measured it,” like Sibawayh’s Arabic example “Zaydan aḍribtuhu.”
rows.anchor: والنصب على: وقدرنا القمر قدرناه، وقد حمله سيبويه على: زيدا أضربته

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ prefers the nominative: after calling the night a sign, the verse makes the sun and moon follow it as two further signs.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: في القمر (¬4) أعجب إلى؛ لأنه قال: {وآية لهم الليل} ثم جعل الشمس والقمر متبعين الليل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda prefers the accusative because it is flanked by the preceding verb naslakh and following qaddarnāhu; he understands “We made it with stations,” omitting a noun.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: النصب أحب إلي؛ للفعل المتقدم قبله والمتأخر بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon’s stations are the familiar twenty-eight positions from the start of the month through its twenty-eighth night; at its final station it dwindles.
rows.anchor: ومنازل القمر معروفة، وهي: ثمانية وعشرون منزلة، من أول الشهر إلى ثمان وعشرين ليلة منه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says al-ʿurjūn is the stem supporting the small branches of a date cluster; when old and dry it becomes thin and small, like the moon at month’s end or first crescent.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (العرجون عود العذق الذي تركبه الشماريخ من العذق

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq derives ʿurjūn from the triliteral root ʿ-r-j and says an old date stem bends and becomes crooked.
rows.anchor: والعرجون على ما ذكر أبو إسحاق من الثلاثي؛ لأنه (¬4) جعل النون زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording compresses the idea that the moon travels through its stations until it returns to the shape of an old date stem; mentioning stations implies its passage through them.
rows.anchor: والآية مختصرة؛ لأن التقدير: فسار في منازله حتى عاد كالعرجون

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī compares it to a dry date stem that has aged through a year and become crooked.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: كالعرجون اليابس قد حال عليه الحول فتوش

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil gives a similar explanation of the dry, aged date stem.
rows.anchor: فتوش (¬1) (¬2). ونحو هذا قال مقاتل (¬3).

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth treats ʿurjūn as a quadriliteral: the base of the date cluster, broad and yellow, resembles the moon when it has dwindled; ʿarjana means depicting date stems.
rows.anchor: وذكره الليث في باب الرباعي فقال: العرجون أصل العذق، وهو أصفر عريض

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba’s phrase muʿarjan witnesses the sense of something depicted in the shape of palm clusters.
rows.anchor: وقال رؤبة: في خدر مياس الدجى معرجن

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil report that the verse was revealed about Meccan polytheists who called the Qurʾān poetry and Muḥammad a poet, sorcerer, and liar; God refuted them.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي (¬2) ومقاتل (¬3): نزلت في مشركي مكة، حين قالوا: إن القرآن شعر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says poetry was not fitting for the Prophet: he could not recite a line or make its meter come out correctly.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد ما (¬4) ينبغي له الشعر، ما كان يروي بيت شعر ولا يقومه مستقيما

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq glosses it as something that does not come easily to him.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: وما يتسهل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yanbaghī derives from seeking: when something sought becomes easy and comes about, it is said to be yanbaghī, as in “I broke it and it broke.”
rows.anchor: وأصل (ينبغي) من قولهم: بغيت الشيء أبغيه، أي: طلبته

rows.speaker: العباس بن مرداس
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet recited al-ʿAbbās b. Mirdās’s line about dividing the spoils of Banū ʿUbayd and did not put it into correct meter.
rows.anchor: فقد روي أنه كان يتمثل بقول العباس بن مرداس فيقول: أتجعل نهبي ونهب العبيد

rows.speaker: عبد بني الحسحاس
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet also quoted a line by ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās with its meter broken.
rows.anchor: وكان يتمثل بقول عبد بني الحسحاس (¬2) يقول: كلي (¬3) الإسلام والشيب للمرء ناهيا

rows.speaker: طرفة
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet quoted Ṭarafa’s line about news coming to one who was not provisioned, and others corrected its meter for him.
rows.anchor: وكان يتكلم ببيت طرفة فيقول: ويأتيك من لم تزود بالأخبار (¬5) # فيعاد عليه مستويا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes say the Prophet could not readily compose a metered line himself, based on the statement that poetry was not fitting for him.
rows.anchor: والمفسرون ذهبوا إلى أنه ما كان يتسهل له أن يأتي ببيت موزون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports also attribute to the Prophet the rajaz phrases “Are you only a finger that has been bloodied?” and “Here I am; truly the life is the life of the Hereafter.”
rows.anchor: وما روي عنه من الأراجز كقوله: "هل أنت إلا أصبع دميت" (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajaz is a kind of speech, not poetry.
rows.anchor: فالرجز جنس من الكلام ليس بشعر

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the verse does not require that the Prophet never quoted poetry; it means he was no poet and that the Qurʾān differs from created speech and Arab meters.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (ليس يوجب هذا أن يكون النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- لم يتمثل ببيت شعر قط

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: On Abū Isḥāq’s explanation, composing poetry on his own was not easy for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وعلى ما ذكر قوله: {وما ينبغي له} معناه: وما يسهل له إنشاء الشعر من قبل نفسه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says “it” refers to the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: القرآن (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses dhikr as an admonition.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: موعظة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the clear Qurʾān contains obligations, legal penalties, and rulings.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: موعظة. {وقرآن مبين} قال: يريد فيه الفرائض والحدود والأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With li-yundhira, the subject is the Qurʾān; readers who use the tāʾ address Muḥammad, who warns through the Qurʾān’s threats.
rows.anchor: {لينذر} أي: القرآن، ومن قرأ بالتاء فهو خطاب للنبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم-

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the living person is a believer.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد مؤمنا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says it means someone whom God knows will be guided.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: من كان مهتديا في علم الله

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says it means someone capable of understanding what is addressed to him; a disbeliever is like a dead person and does not reflect.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: أي من يعقل ما يخاطب به، فإن الكافر كالميت، وإنه لا يتدبر

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī identifies the living as believers because disbelievers are dead, citing 16:26 and 6:122.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الفارسي: (يعني المؤمنين؛ لأن الكفار أموات كما قال {أموات غير أحياء}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān makes the proof binding against the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {ويحق القول} أي: ويجب الحجة بالقرآن على الكافرين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil say “by night” means that passersby sometimes encounter the destroyed towns between Mecca and Syria by day and sometimes at night.
rows.anchor: وهي ما بين مكة والشام، هذا قول ابن عباس ومقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question at the end of the preceding statement means: will you not consider?
rows.anchor: وتم الكلام هاهنا ثم قال: {أفلا تعقلون} فتعتبرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary’s analysis of idh follows its discussion of the two preceding stories.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: {إذ أبق} الكلام في إذ كما ذكرنا في القصتين قبل هذه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abaqa is a slave’s flight from his master.
rows.anchor: وأبق من إباق العبد، وهو هربه من سيده

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil glosses it as “he fled.”
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: يعني إذ فر

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh explains the phrase as a slave fleeing from his Lord; Ibn ʿAbbās gives a similar explanation.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الله: عبد أبق من ربه. ونحو هذا قال ابن عباس

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The exegetes report that Jonah had promised his people punishment; when it was delayed, he left them as though estranged, went toward the sea, and boarded a ship, which is his flight to the laden vessel.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: كان يونس قد وعد قومه العذاب، فلما تأخر عنهم العذاب خرج كالمنشوز عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage links Jonah’s departure to “when he went off angry” in 21:87, whose discussion was treated earlier.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قوله: {إذ ذهب مغاضبا} [الأنبياء: 87] وقد مر الكلام فيه مستقصى

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The scholars of meaning say Jonah is likened to a slave fleeing his master although he knew God could reach him anywhere on land or sea; he fled toward the ship as if seeking refuge in it.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: يفر من ربه كما يفر العبد من سيده لأنه يعلم أن ربه يقدر عليه أين ما كان من بر وبحر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains Ibn’s meaning as moving away or going off; the word is also used of an escaped slave.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: تأويل ابن تباعد أي ذهب (¬6) إليه
